briefing.headline: The simulation predicts that leavers over the next 12 months fall from about 700 to about 358, roughly half. Treat this as a strong signal that the policy would help retention, not as a forecast of the actual figure.
briefing.most_at_risk: No group reacts badly; caregivers (-56%) and long commuters (-54%) gain most because they win back a day of travel and care time, while finance staff and managers voice the most worry that 'same output' will mean squeezing five days of work into four.
risks: Nearly every voice is wary of how 'keep output at today's level' will be measured. If that stays vague or turns into working the same hours faster, the goodwill behind the predicted drop in leaving could turn into burnout and cynicism.
Deadline-bound work does not compress neatly. The finance manager flags month-end close directly, and managers expect the gap to 'quietly become my problem to fix.'

The trial lasts six months, but the simulation measures leaving over 12 months and assumes the benefit holds. If the trial ends or is scaled back, the gain may not last, and withdrawing a well-loved perk could push leaving up. The simulation did not model that scenario.
design_changes: Before launch, agree and publish team-level output measures, drawn up with the teams themselves. Name the work that will be dropped or cut back, such as meetings and low-value reporting, so the trial does not simply squeeze the same work into fewer hours.
Allow flexible or staggered days off and set coverage rules for peak periods like month-end, so finance and other deadline-driven functions are not set up to fail.

Announce a decision date and the criteria for continuing, adjusting or ending the policy after six months. Consider pushing the start back a month or two to give managers time to prepare, rather than launching next month.
briefing.confidence: low: the direction is consistent across all 48 modelled voices and every group, but a near-50% cut that barely varies by group, alongside very high average sentiment (+1.61 of 2), suggests the model may be overstating enthusiasm, so do not rely on the specific number.
